_comment: Per-language security tools `sv` can run, described here rather than in Rust, so adding one is a data change. Three rules shape every entry. First, SARIF only: each tool is asked for SARIF 2.1.0 and nothing else, because one output parser that is trusted is worth more than five that are nearly right, and a tool that cannot emit SARIF is simply not listed yet. Second, a tool that is not installed reports NOT RUN and how to install it — never a clean pass, which is the whole reason this file exists rather than a shell script. Third, `rules` maps the tool's own rule ids to requirements one at a time, and each entry says in `what` what the rule detects. The `what` is not decoration: `crates/sv-check/tests/citations.rs` compares it with the text of every requirement it cites and fails when they share no vocabulary. Every citation in this file was wrong before that guard existed — `V1.2.1` is output encoding and was cited for SQL injection by seven rules — because nothing read the requirement back. A blanket list per tool would credit bandit's SQL rule with everything bandit knows about; a finding whose rule id is not in the map carries no requirement at all, which is a fair thing to be and is shown as such.

adapters.name: Bandit
adapters.note: Bandit has no SARIF formatter of its own; `bandit-sarif-formatter` registers one, which is why the install line names two packages. Bandit installed without it exits with `invalid choice: 'sarif'` and writes nothing, which is reported as not run with that message attached rather than as a clean scan. Bandit also exits non-zero when it finds something, which is not a failure to run: only a missing report counts as that.

B608.what: SQL query built by string formatting or concatenation

B609.what: a shell wildcard passed to an operating system command

B602.what: an operating system command run through a shell (shell=True)

B603.what: an operating system command run from data that may be untrusted

B605.what: a process started through the operating system shell

B606.what: an operating system command run without a shell, from data that may be untrusted

B307.what: eval used to execute code built at runtime

B301.what: pickle used to deserialize data that may be untrusted

B302.what: marshal used to deserialize data that may be untrusted

B506.what: yaml.load used without a safe loader, which deserializes arbitrary objects

B105.what: a password or secret written into the source as a string

B106.what: a password or secret passed as a hard-coded function argument

B107.what: a password or secret as a hard-coded default argument

B303.what: an insecure hash function such as MD5 or SHA1

B324.what: hashlib called with an insecure hash function such as MD5 or SHA1

B501.what: a TLS request made without validating the server certificate

B201.what: a web framework left in debug mode

adapters.name: gosec
adapters.note: gosec resolves `./...` against the working directory, so it is run from inside the app folder rather than given a path.

G201.what: SQL query built with a format string

G202.what: SQL query built by string concatenation

G204.what: an operating system command executed from data that may be untrusted

G101.what: a credential or secret written into the source as a string

G401.what: an insecure hash function such as MD5 or SHA1

G502.what: the DES cipher package imported, which is not an approved cipher

G503.what: the RC4 cipher package imported, which is not an approved cipher

G402.what: a TLS connection made without validating the server certificate

G404.what: a random number generator that is not cryptographically secure

G304.what: a file opened from a path built out of user-submitted input

G107.what: an outbound request made to a URL built from untrusted input, which is server-side request forgery

adapters.name: Brakeman
adapters.note: Brakeman only understands Rails applications. On a Ruby app that is not Rails it exits without a report, which is recorded as not run rather than as nothing found. The rule ids here are taken from Brakeman's documented warning codes and have not been checked against a real SARIF run, because Brakeman cannot be installed in this sandbox. An id that is wrong maps nothing, which shows as a finding carrying no requirement rather than as a wrong one.

BRAKE0001.what: SQL query built by string interpolation or concatenation

BRAKE0002.what: a database query built from user-submitted parameters

BRAKE0013.what: an operating system command executed from user-submitted input

BRAKE0014.what: a shell command built by string interpolation

BRAKE0015.what: a file path built out of user-submitted input

BRAKE0016.what: a database query built by string interpolation

BRAKE0102.what: a credential or secret written into the source as a string

adapters.name: Semgrep
adapters.note: The only entry that reads more than one language, and the only one that fetches its rules from the network the first time it runs. `sv` itself opens no connection; this tool does, which is why it is listed with that said rather than left to be discovered.
